title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Muda, Mura, Muri (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Muda, Mura, Muri: the Three Ms of waste

The Toyota Production System attacks three distinct categories of loss, often called the Three Ms. A top operations leader knows that muda gets all the attention but mura and muri are the upstream causes: chase muda alone and it comes back.

## Muda (waste)

Muda is any activity that consumes resources without creating value for the customer. Lean distinguishes two types. Type One Muda is activity that creates no value but cannot be eliminated immediately given current technologies or assets: an example is a rework or inspection operation you cannot yet remove. Type Two Muda is activity that creates no value and can be eliminated quickly through kaizen, for example unnecessary movement of product between process steps. The practical rule: remove Type Two muda now, work steadily to design out Type One muda.

## Mura (unevenness)

Mura is unevenness in an operation: gyrating production schedules not driven by actual end-customer demand, and uneven work pacing that forces operators to alternate between rushing and waiting. Mura is reduced through level scheduling (heijunka) and by holding a consistent, steady work pace.

## Muri (overburden)

Muri is overburdening equipment or operators by requiring them to run at a harder, faster pace with more force and effort, for a longer period, than the equipment design and appropriate workforce management allow. Muri drives breakdowns, defects, injuries, and burnout.

## How the three interrelate

The three Ms are linked: eliminating one often eliminates the others. In the classic transport example, overloading one truck to save trips (muri) creates uneven flow at the receiving dock (mura) and generates the waste of waiting and rework (muda). The stable countermeasure is heijunka (level scheduling), which smooths demand so neither people nor machines are alternately starved and overloaded. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Jidoka (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Jidoka: automation with a human touch

Jidoka means providing machines and operators the ability to detect when an abnormal condition has occurred and to immediately stop work. It lets an operation build quality into each process (quality at the source) and separate human work from machine work so one operator can run several machines. Jidoka is one of the two pillars of the Toyota Production System; the other is just-in-time.

## Origin: Sakichi Toyoda and the automatic loom

Sakichi Toyoda, founder of the Toyota Group, created the concept in the early 1900s. Previously, if a thread broke, a loom would keep running and churn out mounds of defective fabric, so each machine needed its own watching operator. Toyoda invented a loom that stopped automatically the moment a thread broke, so one operator could oversee many machines at once. Preventing the defect at the instant it occurs, rather than discovering it later, is the heart of jidoka.

## Autonomation

Jidoka is sometimes called autonomation, meaning automation with human intelligence. The equipment is given enough judgment to distinguish good parts from bad autonomously, without being monitored, freeing people for higher-value multiprocess work.

## Stop, and surface the problem

Jidoka highlights the causes of problems because work stops immediately when a problem first occurs. Stopping the line (often signaled by an andon) makes the abnormality visible at once and forces root-cause problem solving instead of letting defects pass downstream. The principle: never let a defect move to the next step. Build quality in rather than inspecting it in afterward. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Just-in-Time Production (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Just-in-Time (JIT) production

Just-in-time is a system of production that makes and delivers just what is needed, just when it is needed, and just in the amount needed. Its goal is the total elimination of waste to achieve the best possible quality, the lowest possible cost and use of resources, and the shortest possible production and delivery lead times. JIT and jidoka are the two pillars of the Toyota Production System.

## The three operating elements

JIT is built on three elements working together:
1. Takt time: the rate at which product must be made in a process to meet customer demand.
2. Continuous flow: producing and moving one item at a time (or a small, consistent batch) through a series of steps as continuously as possible, with each step making only what the next step requires.
3. Pull system: a method of production control in which downstream activities signal their needs to upstream activities, so nothing is produced until the customer (internal or external) actually requests it. Kanban signals are the common tool for this.

## Heijunka as the foundation

JIT relies on heijunka (production leveling) as its foundation. Without leveling demand, a pure pull system would transmit every spike and dip straight upstream, recreating mura and muri.

## History

The concept originated with Kiichiro Toyoda in the 1930s, with practical implementation beginning around 1949 to 1950 under Taiichi Ohno. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Standardized Work (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Standardized work

Standardized work means establishing precise procedures for each operator's work in a production process, based on three elements:
1. Takt time: the rate at which products must be made in a process to meet customer demand.
2. The precise work sequence in which an operator performs tasks within takt time.
3. The standard inventory (standard in-process stock), including units held in machines, required to keep the process operating smoothly.

## Standardized work is the baseline for kaizen

Once established and displayed at the workstation, standardized work becomes the object of continuous improvement through kaizen. This is the crucial and most misunderstood point: a standard is not a straitjacket, it is the current best-known method and the baseline against which every improvement is measured. Taiichi Ohno's maxim captures it: where there is no standard, there can be no kaizen. If the method drifts or varies operator to operator, you cannot tell whether a change actually improved anything, because there is no stable reference. So standardize first, then improve the standard, then re-standardize. Standardized work also exposes abnormalities immediately: when the actual work departs from the documented sequence or in-process stock, the deviation is visible at a glance. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Heijunka / Production Leveling (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Heijunka: leveling production

Heijunka is leveling the type and quantity of production over a fixed period of time. It lets a plant meet customer demand efficiently while minimizing inventory, capital cost, labor, and production lead time across the value stream. Heijunka is the foundation that makes a just-in-time pull system stable.

## Leveling by volume

Production quantity is smoothed across the period. If a producer receives 500 orders a week arriving unevenly (200 Monday, 100 Tuesday, 50 Wednesday, 100 Thursday, 50 Friday), it can instead build a level 100 units per day, holding a small buffer of finished goods near shipping to absorb the daily swings. This protects the upstream processes from the customer's day-to-day volatility.

## Leveling by product type or mix

Rather than mass-producing one model in a big batch, the producer sequences different models through the period. A shirt maker with weekly demand of 5 of Model A, 3 of Model B, and 2 each of Models C and D would replace the batch sequence A A A A A B B B C C D D with a repeating mixed pattern such as A A B C D A A B C D A B, adjusted as orders change. Mixed sequencing shortens the replenishment interval for every model.

## The heijunka box

A heijunka box is a visual scheduling tool: product types on one axis, time intervals on the other, with kanban cards slotted to pace the leveled sequence so operators can execute it at a glance.

## Why it matters

Heijunka directly counters mura (unevenness) and muri (overburden). Batch-and-queue by contrast expands lead time, inflates work-in-process, propagates a defect across a whole batch before it is caught, and strains workers with alternating idle and rush periods. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, 5S (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## 5S: workplace organization and visual control

5S refers to five related terms, each beginning with an S sound, describing workplace practices conducive to visual control and lean production. The point is not tidiness for its own sake: a workplace organized so that the normal condition is obvious makes any abnormality visible instantly, which is the precondition for standard work and continuous improvement.

## The five terms

1. Seiri (Sort): separate needed from unneeded items, tools, parts, materials, paperwork, and discard the unneeded.
2. Seiton (Straighten, or Set in order): neatly arrange what is left, a place for everything and everything in its place.
3. Seiso (Shine): clean and wash; inspect through cleaning so deterioration and leaks are caught early.
4. Seiketsu (Standardize): the cleanliness and order that result from regularly performing the first three Ss, made into a repeatable standard.
5. Shitsuke (Sustain): the discipline to keep performing the first four Ss so gains do not decay.

## The sixth S

Some lean practitioners add a sixth S for Safety: establish and practice safety procedures in the workshop and office.

## Why it matters

5S creates standards that reveal problems, supports the basic stability needed to sustain incremental gains, reduces waste in all forms, and builds a disciplined workplace where teams can focus on value-creating work. The common failure is treating 5S as a one-time cleanup event rather than a sustained daily discipline. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, PDCA / Plan-Do-Check-Act (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## PDCA: the improvement cycle

PDCA is an improvement cycle based on the scientific method of proposing a change in a process, implementing the change, measuring the results, and taking appropriate action. It is also called the Deming Cycle or Deming Wheel, after W. Edwards Deming, who introduced it in Japan in the 1950s. It evolved from Walter Shewhart's earlier improvement cycle. PDCA is the foundation of continuous improvement, or kaizen.

## The four steps

1. Plan: determine goals for a process and the changes needed to achieve them. State a hypothesis and predict what will happen.
2. Do: implement the changes, ideally as a small, controlled experiment.
3. Check: evaluate the results against the prediction and the performance target. (In the PDSA variant, this step is Study, emphasizing that you learn from the gap between prediction and result, not just pass or fail it.)
4. Act: if the change worked, standardize and stabilize it as the new standard work; if not, begin the cycle again with what you learned.

## Why it matters

PDCA turns improvement into disciplined experimentation rather than opinion-driven change. Leaders set targets, teams run improvements, results are measured against objectives, and successful changes become standardized work so the gain holds. The classic anti-pattern is skipping Check and Act: teams launch changes (plenty of Plan-Do) but never verify the effect or lock in the win, so improvements neither prove out nor stick. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, 5 Whys Root Cause Analysis (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## 5 Whys: reaching the root cause

5 Whys is the practice of asking why repeatedly whenever a problem is encountered, in order to get beyond the obvious symptoms and discover the root cause. It originates with Taiichi Ohno and the Toyota Production System. The specific number five is not the point: the point is to keep asking why until the root cause is reached and eliminated, so the problem cannot recur.

## Taiichi Ohno's machine example

Ohno illustrated the technique with a machine that stopped:
1. Why did the machine stop? A fuse blew because of an overload.
2. Why was there an overload? The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated.
3. Why was it not lubricated enough? The lubrication pump was not pumping sufficiently.
4. Why was it not pumping sufficiently? The pump shaft was worn and rattling.
5. Why was the shaft worn? There was no strainer attached, so metal scraps got in.

Stopping at why two or three (replace the fuse, replace the bearing) fixes the symptom and the machine breaks again. Only the fifth why, install a strainer, prevents recurrence.

## Practicing it well

To use 5 Whys correctly you must first have a clear mental picture of how the process should work and be able to identify exactly where it is misbehaving. It is logic-based root cause analysis: it requires disciplined critical thinking but no advanced mathematics. The aim is always to prevent the problem from recurring by eliminating its underlying cause, not merely to replace the part that failed. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Theory of Constraints (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Theory of Constraints (TOC)

The Theory of Constraints is a management philosophy and a set of tools for organizational change developed by the Israeli physicist Dr. Eliyahu Goldratt and popularized in his 1984 business novel The Goal. TOC concentrates on improving profit by managing constraints, the factors that prevent a company from achieving its goal.

## Constraint thinking

Every system has at least one constraint, a single bottleneck that limits the throughput of the whole. Improving anywhere other than the constraint does not increase system output; it only creates more inventory or idle capacity. So TOC's primary focus is removing or managing the constraint to improve throughput, whereas lean focuses on identifying and removing waste to improve the flow of value. Both lean and TOC emphasize improving the whole system rather than optimizing individual parts, which is the central discipline that separates real operations leaders from local cost-cutters.

## Relationship to lean

The two philosophies are complementary. Lean makes flow smooth and removes waste everywhere; TOC tells you where in the value stream to concentrate first (the constraint) so that improvement effort converts directly into money. An hour saved at a non-constraint is a mirage; an hour saved at the constraint is an hour of extra throughput for the entire system. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: W. Edwards Deming Institute, Deming's 14 Points for Management
text:
## Deming's 14 Points for Management

W. Edwards Deming's 14 Points are the foundation of transforming management for quality. They locate the causes of poor quality in the system, which management owns, not in the individual worker.

1. Create constancy of purpose toward improvement of product and service, with the aim to become competitive, stay in business, and provide jobs.
2. Adopt the new philosophy. Management must awaken to the challenge, learn its responsibilities, and take on leadership for change.
3. Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality. Eliminate the need for mass inspection by building quality into the product in the first place.
4. End the practice of awarding business on price tag alone. Minimize total cost by moving toward a single supplier for any one item, on a long-term relationship of loyalty and trust.
5. Improve constantly and forever the system of production and service, to improve quality and productivity, and thus constantly decrease costs.
6. Institute training on the job.
7. Institute leadership. The aim of supervision should be to help people and machines do a better job.
8. Drive out fear, so that everyone may work effectively for the company.
9. Break down barriers between departments so research, design, sales, and production work as one team.
10. Eliminate slogans, exhortations, and targets asking the workforce for zero defects and new productivity levels, since the bulk of causes of low quality belong to the system and lie beyond the workforce's power.
11a. Eliminate work standards (quotas) on the factory floor. Substitute leadership.
11b. Eliminate management by objective and management by numbers or numerical goals. Substitute leadership.
12. Remove the barriers that rob workers, and people in management and engineering, of their right to pride of workmanship. This means abolishing the annual merit rating and management by objective.
13. Institute a vigorous program of education and self-improvement.
14. Put everybody in the company to work to accomplish the transformation. The transformation is everybody's job.

## Why an operations leader keeps these close

Points 10, 11, and 12 are the ones most violated in modern operations: numerical quotas, slogans, and merit ratings push people to hit a number by gaming the system rather than improving it. Deming's insight is that exhorting workers to do better cannot fix a system only management can change. Attribution: The W. Edwards Deming Institute.

title: TOC Institute, The Five Focusing Steps (Process of Ongoing Improvement)
text:
## The Five Focusing Steps (POOGI)

Goldratt's Theory of Constraints improves a system through a repeating cycle called the Process of Ongoing Improvement. The guiding image is a chain: the strength of a chain is set by its weakest link, so strengthening any link other than the weakest is a waste of time and energy.

## The five steps

1. Identify the system's constraint. Locate the single limiting factor that currently restricts the whole system's output. Strengthening any link apart from the weakest is wasted effort.
2. Exploit the constraint. Squeeze as much as possible out of it. Maximize the utilization and productivity of the constraint resource before spending any money, for example stop letting the bottleneck sit idle at lunch or process defects, and make sure it only ever works on good, needed parts.
3. Subordinate everything else to the constraint. Align all other processes and policies to support the constraint. Non-constraints must not produce more than the constraint can handle, and must guarantee the constraint never starves for material or attention. This is the step managers hate, because it means deliberately running non-bottlenecks below their full capacity.
4. Elevate the constraint. Only once exploitation and subordination are exhausted do you expand capacity by investing: buy equipment, add a shift, hire people, offload work.
5. Prevent inertia from becoming the constraint. Once elevated, the old weak link may no longer be weakest; a new constraint appears elsewhere. Return to Step 1 and begin the cycle again, and never let policy or habit (inertia) silently become the new constraint.

## Why it matters

The five steps encode the anti-local-optimization discipline: you do not improve everywhere at once, you concentrate on the one place that governs system output, then move to the next. Attribution: TOC Institute.

title: W. Edwards Deming Institute, The System of Profound Knowledge (SoPK)
text:
## The System of Profound Knowledge

The System of Profound Knowledge ties together Dr. Deming's seminal theories and teachings on quality, management, and leadership into four interrelated areas. The Institute warns that often minor pieces of what he taught are presented as the total of what he taught: the tools (control charts, PDSA) are only useful inside the whole system of thought. The four parts interact; none can be fully understood in isolation.

## 1. Appreciation for a system

An organization is a network of interdependent components that work together to try to accomplish the aim of the system. Management's job is to optimize the whole system, not the separate parts. Optimizing a part (a department, a metric, a shift) almost always sub-optimizes the whole. Every system must have an aim; without an aim there is no system.

## 2. Knowledge about variation

All work is a process, and all processes vary. The critical distinction is between common-cause variation (inherent, stable, built into the process itself) and special-cause variation (unusual, assignable, from outside the normal process). Treating a common-cause result as if it had a special cause, or the reverse, makes things worse. This is the root of Deming's warning against tampering.

## 3. Theory of knowledge

Management is prediction. Any plan or rational decision requires prediction based on theory, and knowledge is built by revising theory against observation. There is no knowledge without theory, and no learning without a way to compare prediction to result (the basis of PDSA).

## 4. Psychology

People are motivated intrinsically and extrinsically. Understanding people, their interactions, and the way fear and extrinsic rewards can destroy intrinsic motivation and pride of workmanship is essential to leading a system. Attribution: The W. Edwards Deming Institute.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Poka-Yoke / Mistake-Proofing (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Poka-yoke: error-proofing

Poka-yoke is a Japanese term meaning error-proofing, achieved by implementing simple and inexpensive devices that help operators avoid mistakes. Poka means an inadvertent error, and yoke means prevention. The aim is 100% quality by finding and preventing defects at their source, so no operator can pass a defect forward and the problem is solved permanently rather than sorted out later.

## Why not rely on inspection

Quality by sampling inspection guarantees that some defects will be missed. Full 100% inspection by a human is costly and still fallible. Poka-yoke instead builds the check into the process itself, so the error is caught (or made impossible) the moment it would occur.

## Two approaches

1. Control (shutdown): the most powerful method. The process physically cannot proceed when something is wrong, for example a machine will not start if the workpiece is set incorrectly, or an assembly step is blocked by a photocell until the previous part is present.
2. Warning: the device alerts the operator to an abnormal condition with a buzzer or a light, but relies on the human to react.

## Examples

Physical designs that only fit one way so a part cannot be installed backwards, photocells that stop progression to the next stage, a car's blind-spot warning, and a washing machine door that locks before the drum spins. The design principle: make it impossible, or at least hard, to do the wrong thing. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Takt Time (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Takt time: the heartbeat of production

Takt time is the available production time divided by customer demand. It is the rate at which a finished unit must be completed to exactly meet customer demand, no faster and no slower. The purpose of takt time is to precisely match production with demand; it provides the heartbeat of a lean production system.

## The formula and a worked example

Takt time = available production time / customer demand. If a factory runs 480 minutes per day and customers demand 240 widgets per day, takt time is 480 / 240 = 2 minutes: one finished widget must come off the line every two minutes. The unit scales: if customers want two new products per month, the takt time is two weeks.

## Origin and use

The word takt comes from German, meaning a precise interval of time such as a musical meter or beat. It was first used as a production management tool in the German aircraft industry in the 1930s. Toyota adopted it widely in the 1950s, reviewing takt monthly and adjusting it about every 10 days as demand changes.

## Why it matters

Takt time converts demand into a physical rhythm the whole line can be balanced to. Producing faster than takt overproduces (waste and inventory); slower than takt fails to meet demand. Balancing every station's work content to just under takt is the core of line design and standardized work. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Kanban (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Kanban: the pull signal

A kanban is a signaling device that gives authorization and instructions for the production or withdrawal (conveyance) of items in a pull system. The term is Japanese for sign or signboard. Kanban is the practical mechanism that makes a just-in-time pull system work: no parts are produced or moved in the absence of a kanban.

## Types

Production kanban tells an upstream process to make a specific quantity for the downstream process. Withdrawal (or conveyance) kanban authorizes the movement of material and exists as an internal interprocess kanban or a supplier kanban, so conveyance happens only when actually needed.

## Physical form

A kanban can be a card, a triangular metal plate, a colored ball, an empty container, or an electronic signal, whatever reliably carries the information and cannot give a false instruction.

## Rules and WIP control

Kanban operates under a fixed set of rules (the six rules of kanban), the essence of which is that a downstream process withdraws only what it needs, an upstream process produces only what has been withdrawn, no defective part is ever passed along, and the number of kanban is gradually reduced to expose problems. Because production or movement requires an authorized signal, the total number of kanban in circulation sets a hard cap on work-in-process: fewer cards means less inventory and tighter flow. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Continuous Flow / One-Piece Flow (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Continuous flow

Continuous flow means producing and moving one item at a time (or a small and consistent batch of items) through a series of processing steps as continuously as possible, with each step making just what is requested by the next step. It is also called make one move one, one-piece flow, or single-piece flow. It can be realized with an automated moving line or a manual work cell.

## Contrast with batch-and-queue

The alternative is batch-and-queue: making a large batch at one step, then queuing it before the next. Continuous flow is a deliberate departure from big-batch production. Each step produces only what the next step requests, which prevents overproduction.

## Why smaller batches win

Moving one piece at a time collapses lead time: instead of waiting for an entire batch to finish before anything moves, the first good unit reaches the next step almost immediately. It also exposes problems fast: if a defect appears, it is caught at the next operation within seconds instead of being replicated across a whole batch and discovered much later. Smaller batches mean less work-in-process, less space, less cash tied up, and far shorter feedback loops for quality. The counterintuitive lesson experienced operators internalize: bigger batches feel efficient locally but lengthen total lead time and hide defects. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, A3 Report / A3 Problem Solving (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## A3 report and A3 thinking

The A3 is named for the international paper size (297mm by 420mm, the same as the US 11-by-17-inch tabloid sheet). Pioneered at Toyota, an A3 forces an entire problem-solving story, root cause analysis and countermeasures included, onto a single sheet, often with graphics.

## A3 is a management process, not just a form

Crucially, the A3 is a management process learned through dialogue about concrete problems between a lean manager and the person owning the problem. The mentor coaches by asking questions rather than giving answers, developing the problem-solver's lean thinking while keeping responsibility with them.

## The structure (left side to right side, following PDCA)

The left side of the sheet lays out the elements of the problem or current condition; the right side lays out the countermeasures considered, tested, and chosen. A full A3 walks through: the current situation, the nature of the issue, the range of possible countermeasures, the best countermeasure, the means (who will do what by when) to put it into practice, and the evidence that the issue has actually been addressed. This maps directly onto Plan-Do-Check-Act. The discipline of one page prevents the common failure of jumping to a solution before the problem and its root cause are understood. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Gemba and the Gemba Walk (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Gemba: go to the actual place

Gemba is the Japanese term for the actual place, often used for the shop floor or any place where value-creating work actually occurs. The core management belief is that you cannot understand a problem from a conference room or a dashboard; you have to go to where the work is done and observe it directly.

## The gemba walk

A gemba walk is a management practice for grasping the current situation through direct observation and inquiry before taking action. Leaders go to the gemba to raise consciousness about improvement possibilities and to assess whether the management system is stable enough to be a basis for improvement. The famous phrasing associated with the practice is go see, ask why, show respect.

## Genchi genbutsu

Japanese companies complement gemba with genchi genbutsu, essentially go and see for yourself, to emphasize the importance of empiricism: decisions are grounded in firsthand facts, not reports or assumptions. The anti-pattern this guards against is management by dashboard, deciding from summarized numbers without ever seeing the real conditions that produced them. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Pull Production (Lean Lexicon)
text:
## Pull production

Pull production is a method of production control in which downstream activities signal their needs to upstream activities, so nothing is made until a real downstream customer requests it. Its purpose is to eliminate overproduction, the worst of the wastes, and it is a core component of just-in-time.

## Push versus pull

Push production works the opposite way: upstream processes build to a forecast and schedule regardless of actual downstream demand, which reliably creates inventory buildup, obsolescence, and the illusion of productivity. Pull reverses the trigger: the downstream operation withdraws what it needs (typically via kanban), and only then does the upstream operation replenish.

## Three types of pull system

1. Supermarket (replenishment or fill-up) pull: each process holds a small stock of its outputs in a defined location; a downstream withdrawal triggers an upstream signal to replenish. Simple to manage but requires carrying every part number.
2. Sequential (made-to-order) pull: used when part numbers are too many to hold in a supermarket. Kanban are released in a strict sequence and each process makes items in that order. Minimizes inventory but demands short, predictable lead times and strong discipline.
3. Mixed pull: combines both, often via an 80/20 split, supermarket logic for high-runners and sequential for low-volume specials. Balances complexity and inventory but requires strict operational discipline. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute Lean Lexicon.

title: Vorne, OEE.com, Overall Equipment Effectiveness: Definition and Calculation
text:
## OEE: Overall Equipment Effectiveness

OEE is the percentage of manufacturing time that is truly productive. An OEE score of 100% means you are manufacturing only good parts, as fast as possible, with no stop time. It is the single best gauge of how well a production asset is actually used.

## The three factors

OEE is the product of three factors, each a percentage: OEE = Availability x Performance x Quality.
- Availability = Run Time / Planned Production Time. It accounts for all stops, both unplanned (breakdowns) and planned (changeovers). 100% means the process never stopped during scheduled time.
- Performance = (Ideal Cycle Time x Total Count) / Run Time. It accounts for slow cycles and minor stops. 100% means the process ran at its maximum rated speed whenever it was running.
- Quality = Good Count / Total Count. It accounts for defects and rework. 100% means every part was good the first time.

## Benchmarks

100% OEE is perfect production. 85% OEE is considered world-class for discrete manufacturers. 60% is fairly typical, and 40% is not uncommon for plants just starting to measure. The number itself matters less than the trend and the loss breakdown it drives.

## Worked example

A shift of 480 minutes with 60 minutes of breaks gives 420 minutes of Planned Production Time. With 47 minutes of downtime, Run Time is 373 minutes. Ideal cycle time is 1.0 second, total output is 19,271 widgets, of which 423 are rejects, leaving 18,848 good. Then Availability = 373 / 420 = 88.81%, Performance = (1.0 s x 19,271) / (373 x 60 s) = 86.11%, Quality = 18,848 / 19,271 = 97.80%, and OEE = 0.8881 x 0.8611 x 0.9780 = 74.79%.

## Six Big Losses and TEEP

OEE decomposes into the Six Big Losses (breakdowns and setup/adjustments hit Availability; small stops and reduced speed hit Performance; startup rejects and production rejects hit Quality), which turn a single score into a targeted improvement list. TEEP (Total Effective Equipment Performance) extends OEE by multiplying it by Utilization (Planned Production Time / All Time), measuring performance against all 168 hours in a week rather than only scheduled time. Attribution: Vorne, OEE.com.

title: John Doerr / What Matters, OKRs: Objectives and Key Results
text:
## OKRs: Objectives and Key Results

OKR stands for Objectives and Key Results, a collaborative goal-setting methodology used by teams and individuals to set challenging, ambitious goals with measurable results. It is the operating cadence that connects strategy to weekly execution.

## Objective and Key Results

The Objective is what you want to accomplish: significant, concrete, action-oriented, and ideally inspirational. Objectives are qualitative. The Key Results are how you measure progress toward the objective: specific, time-bound, and aggressive yet realistic, with measurable, verifiable outcomes. Key Results are quantitative. If a Key Result does not have a number, it is not a Key Result.

## The formula

The canonical structure is: I will (Objective) as measured by (Key Results). Example: I will fix the website for the vast majority of people as measured by 7 out of 10 people being able to get through, a 1-second response time, and a 1% error rate.

## Origin and best practices

Andy Grove developed the methodology at Intel; John Doerr introduced OKRs to Google's founders in 1999, and Google adopted it as its planning model. Best practice is a small number of Objectives, each with about 3 to 5 Key Results, set on a quarterly cycle. OKRs deliberately favor ambitious stretch goals: for aspirational OKRs, scoring around 70% (0.7 out of 1.0) is considered success, because a team that hits 100% every time set its targets too low. The related anti-pattern is treating OKRs as a top-down performance quota, which recreates exactly the fear-and-sandbagging dynamic Deming warned against. Attribution: John Doerr, What Matters (whatmatters.com).

title: Joe The IT Guy, Watermelon SLAs (Anti-Pattern)
text:
## Anti-pattern: watermelon metrics

A watermelon SLA (or watermelon metric) is a measure that reports green on the outside but is red on the inside: the dashboard says the target is met while the operation has left a trail of unhappy customers. Every SLA is green, every report is signed off, and the users are still furious. Recognizing this is a hallmark of a genuine operations leader, because it is the most common way a metrics program lies to management.

## Why every metric can be green and the customer still unhappy

Consider a payroll system with a 99.5% availability target. The SLA can be fully met on paper even if the entire allowed downtime landed squarely on month-end processing, when payroll actually needed to run. Hitting the number gives no assurance the customer experienced good service or that the business need was met. The metric measured the wrong thing.

## Root cause: measuring activity instead of outcomes

The failure is a measurement-philosophy failure, and two laws name it. Goodhart's Law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Campbell's Law: once a metric is identified as the primary indicator of success, its ability to accurately measure success tends to be compromised. When SLAs become a box-ticking exercise that rewards speed over quality, analysts skip proper documentation and knowledge-base checks to hit response times, which actually lowers first-contact resolution. The metric improves while the service degrades.

## Countermeasure

Shift from measuring internal activity and technical targets to measuring business impact and actual customer experience (the idea behind experience-level agreements, or XLAs). Pair every efficiency metric with an outcome metric (for example a rising ticket reopen rate exposes the truth a green SLA is hiding), so no single number can be gamed in isolation. Attribution: Joe The IT Guy.

title: W. Edwards Deming Institute, The Funnel Experiment / Tampering (Anti-Pattern)
text:
## Anti-pattern: tampering (over-adjusting a stable process)

Deming's Funnel Experiment was devised to demonstrate the adverse effects of making changes to a process without first carefully studying the sources of variation. Deming called this worsening tampering. It is one of the most expensive mistakes an operations manager can make, because it feels like responsible management while it actively degrades the process.

## The setup

Drop a marble through a funnel onto a paper target, trying to get the marble to stop as close to the target as possible. There is natural variation in where the marble lands. The question is how the operator should adjust the funnel between drops.

## The four rules

1. Rule 1: leave the funnel alone, fixed over the target, never adjust it.
2. Rule 2: after each drop, move the funnel from its current position by an amount opposite to the error (compensate for the last miss).
3. Rule 3: after each drop, reset the funnel to the target, adjusting from the target by the opposite of the last error.
4. Rule 4: set the funnel directly over wherever the last marble landed (chase the process).

Rule 1 produces the least variation and the tightest cluster around the target. Every rule that reacts to individual results makes variation worse; Rules 2 and 3 widen the spread, and Rule 4 causes the pattern to wander ever further from the target without bound.

## Tampering defined

Tampering is treating a common cause of variation as if it were a special cause, or the reverse. If anyone adjusts a stable process in reaction to a single undesirable result, or even an unusually good result, the output that follows will be worse than if the process had been left alone.

## Management applications

The same error shows up as adjusting a process after one out-of-range point, changing policy from a single survey, resetting quotas or budgets to the latest actual, and reacting to the newest data point as though it were a signal. The disciplined response is to distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation (typically with a control chart) before acting, and to improve the system rather than jerk it around. Attribution: The W. Edwards Deming Institute.

title: Lean Enterprise Institute, Lean Is Not Traditional Cost-Cutting (Myth-Busting)
text:
## Myth: lean means cutting costs by cutting people and capacity

A persistent and damaging myth is that lean is a cost-cutting or headcount-reduction program (leaning out the workforce). The Lean Enterprise Institute is explicit: lean is not a short-term cost-cutting methodology, and long-term financial improvement is an outcome of a lean strategy, not its primary objective. Confusing the two is how lean initiatives destroy trust and then fail.

## Cost-cutting versus cost-improvement

Cost-cutting is periodic, often unsustainable reduction made to balance a budget or hit a short-term number, frequently misaligned with strategy. Cost-improvement is the methodical identification of value-added versus non-value-added activity, systematically eliminating waste while improving quality and delivery. Lean does the second, which lowers cost as a byproduct of removing waste, and refuses the first.

## Respect for people and the no-layoff principle

The engine of lean is that everyone in the organization drives waste out of their own work. That engine stops the instant people believe improving their process will eliminate their job: how can you ask people to expose and remove waste, freeing up capacity, if the reward is that they or their colleagues get laid off? So capacity freed by kaizen is redeployed strategically, not cashed in as layoffs. A common lean commitment is telling the team up front that there will be no layoffs as a result of kaizen activity.

## Ohno's stance

Rather than being creative with accounting, Taiichi Ohno advocated reducing cost by being creative in how we look at the work, to find ways to make it easier, better, and faster. The point is to grow capacity and value, not to shrink the organization. Attribution: Lean Enterprise Institute, The Lean Post.

title: Businessmap (Kanbanize), Little's Law
text:
## Little's Law: the flow equation

Little's Law describes the relationship between the three fundamental flow metrics of any stable system. In operations and kanban form it is: WIP = Throughput x Cycle Time, where WIP is the number of work items in progress, Throughput is the rate at which items are completed, and Cycle Time is the average time an item spends in the process. Rearranged, Cycle Time = WIP / Throughput.

## What it means

The law is powerful because it holds for any stable queue regardless of the details. It says you have only three levers and they are locked together: if you want shorter cycle time (faster delivery) without adding capacity, you must reduce WIP. A worked example: a bakery serving 120 customers per hour with an average 5-minute wait has, on average, 120 x (5/60) = 10 customers in the system at once.

## Anti-pattern: too much WIP and the illusion of high utilization

The most common flow mistake operations managers make is starting more work to look busy and keep everyone 100% utilized. Little's Law shows exactly why that backfires: with throughput fixed by capacity, piling on WIP directly and proportionally increases cycle time, so everything takes longer and predictability collapses. Kanban practice therefore limits work in progress to keep the arrival and departure of work stable, which shortens lead time, improves forecasting, and surfaces bottlenecks. Stable flow, not maximal busyness, is the goal: if you know how flow works, then you know how value delivery works. Attribution: Businessmap (Kanbanize).

title: SixSigma.us, Six Sigma DPMO and DMAIC
text:
## Six Sigma: DPMO and the 3.4 target

Six Sigma is a data-driven quality methodology whose defining goal is a process so capable that it produces no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities (DPMO). That equals 99.99966% accuracy, near-perfect quality. Sigma refers to the standard deviation of a process: a six-sigma process fits six standard deviations between the process mean and the nearest specification limit, so even normal variation almost never crosses into defect territory.

## DPMO formula

DPMO offers a standardized way to quantify defects across processes of different complexity: DPMO = (Number of defects / (Number of units x Opportunities per unit)) x 1,000,000. Counting opportunities per unit, not just units, lets a simple part and a complex assembly be compared on the same scale. DPMO is used within statistical process control to baseline a process, track improvement over time, and prioritize where defect reduction matters most.

## DMAIC

Six Sigma improvement projects run the DMAIC cycle: Define the problem, goal, and customer requirements; Measure the current process and collect data to establish a baseline; Analyze the data to find the root causes of defects; Improve the process by designing and testing solutions that address those root causes; Control the improved process with monitoring (such as control charts) so the gains hold and the process does not drift back. DMAIC is the disciplined, evidence-first backbone that keeps Six Sigma from becoming opinion-driven change. Attribution: SixSigma.us.
